title: The Arday Case Is a Test for Academia
author: Oliver Traldi
content:
![The Arday Case Is a Test for
Academia](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-23-at-10.10.01
---PM-1-1.png)

Academia is a place where very awkward people impose strict standards on one
another. But these standards are localized, imposed by disciplines and
departments. One group's standards might be opaque to the rest of the
university, not to mention the outside world. What passes for good scholarship
in one discipline might seem ridiculous in another.

The current crisis of the university can be traced partly to two types of
attacks on these already precarious standards. The first has been the
introduction of new disciplines that appear to have virtually no standards at
all; the second is the relaxation of standards within the disciplines to
accommodate new entrants and trendy topics. New interpersonal standards of
emotional sensitivity and demographic inclusion have increasingly taken the
place of intellectual standards of clever argumentation and strong evidence.
But the enforcement of those new metrics turns out to be just as awkward and
strict as what preceded them. Paradoxically, the harsh imposition of the new
standards often is**** as insensitive and exclusionary as what came before.

The incompatibility of these two sets of standards accounts for at least some
of the media firestorm around the late Jason Arday's plagiarism and
fabrications, and the subsequent focus on Nathan Cofnas, the Ghent University
postdoc and whistleblower. Cofnas authored the initial
[_article_](https://substack.com/@nathancofnas/p-207415162?ref=compactmag.com)
outlining apparently longstanding doubts about Arday's scholarly and
extramural accomplishments. Arday and Cofnas in some respects exemplify the
broader shift in academic standards.
